question_html: Under the LLP Act, 2008, how does the LLP's own liability for its obligations differ from the liability of its individual partners?

options.A: The LLP itself, being a separate legal entity, is liable to the full extent of its own assets for its obligations, whereas the liability of the partners is limited to the extent of their agreed capital contribution to the LLP
options.B: Both the LLP and its partners are liable only to the extent of the partners' agreed capital contribution, with the LLP's own assets beyond that contribution being insulated from all claims
options.C: The LLP has no independent liability of its own; all obligations of the LLP are, by default, the personal and unlimited liability of each individual partner, exactly as in a traditional partnership firm
options.D: The liability of the LLP and of its partners is identical and co-extensive in every respect, with no distinction drawn between the entity's assets and the partners' individual capital contributions

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The LLP itself, being a separate legal entity, is liable to the full extent of its own assets for its obligations, whereas the liability of the partners is limited to the extent of their agreed capital contribution to the LLP

The defining feature of an LLP is this liability split - the LLP answers for its obligations out of the whole of its own assets, while each partner's exposure is capped at the amount he agreed to contribute, giving partners the limited-liability protection associated with a company while preserving partnership-style internal flexibility.

question_html: What gap in the pre-existing legal landscape did the LLP Act, 2008 aim to fill, and which class of persons was this new form particularly designed to serve?

options.A: The LLP Act, 2008 was enacted solely to replace the Companies Act, 2013 as the governing statute for all business entities in India, eliminating the traditional partnership and company forms entirely
options.B: Lawmakers felt the need for an alternative to the traditional partnership (which carries unlimited personal liability) on the one hand, and the statute-based governance structure of a limited liability company on the other; the LLP form was designed to enable professional expertise and entrepreneurial initiative to operate in a flexible, innovative, and efficient manner, making it particularly suited to entrepreneurs, professionals, and enterprises providing services or engaged in scientific/technical disciplines, as well as small enterprises and venture capital investment
options.C: The LLP form was designed exclusively for large, publicly listed multinational corporations seeking to reduce their regulatory compliance burden, with no particular relevance to small enterprises or professional service providers
options.D: The LLP Act, 2008 was enacted purely to formalize existing partnership firms without offering any liability protection beyond what the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 already provided

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Lawmakers felt the need for an alternative to the traditional partnership (which carries unlimited personal liability) on the one hand, and the statute-based governance structure of a limited liability company on the other; the LLP form was designed to enable professional expertise and entrepreneurial initiative to operate in a flexible, innovative, and efficient manner, making it particularly suited to entrepreneurs, professionals, and enterprises providing services or engaged in scientific/technical disciplines, as well as small enterprises and venture capital investment

The LLP form deliberately sits between two poles - unlimited-liability traditional partnerships and heavily statute-governed limited companies - combining the benefits of limited liability with partnership-style flexibility, making it a natural fit for professionals (who previously feared unlimited liability), entrepreneurs, small enterprises, and venture-capital-backed ventures.

question_html: When did the LLP Act, 2008 come into force, to what territory does it extend, how many sections and Schedules does it have, and does the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 apply to LLPs?

options.A: The LLP Act, 2008 came into force on 12th December, 2008 (the date of Parliamentary passage) and applies only to the states in which a LLP's registered office happens to be situated, with 6 Schedules and full applicability of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
options.B: The LLP Act, 2008 came into force on 7th January, 2009 (the date of Presidential assent) and has only 2 Schedules; the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies concurrently to LLPs in full, alongside the LLP Act's own provisions
options.C: The LLP Act, 2008 came into force on 31st March, 2009 and extends to the whole of India; it has 81 sections (of which section 81 now stands omitted with effect from 1st April, 2022) and 4 Schedules; the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does NOT apply to LLPs, save as otherwise provided [Section 4]
options.D: The LLP Act, 2008 extends only to Union Territories and not to the States of India, with 81 sections but no Schedules at all governing conversion or mutual rights and duties

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The LLP Act, 2008 came into force on 31st March, 2009 and extends to the whole of India; it has 81 sections (of which section 81 now stands omitted with effect from 1st April, 2022) and 4 Schedules; the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does NOT apply to LLPs, save as otherwise provided [Section 4]

While the LLP Bill was passed by Parliament on 12th December, 2008 and received Presidential assent on 7th January, 2009, the Act itself came into force (commencement notification) on 31st March, 2009, extending to the whole of India, with 81 sections (section 81 now omitted) and 4 Schedules; section 4 expressly excludes the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 from applying to LLPs.

question_html: Under section 2(1)(d), 'body corporate' means a company as defined in section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013 and includes which three categories, while excluding which three categories?

options.A: It includes a corporation sole, a co-operative society, and the Government, while excluding any LLP registered under this Act, any LLP incorporated outside India, and any company incorporated outside India - the reverse of the actual inclusion/exclusion scheme
options.B: 'Body corporate' is confined strictly to companies incorporated in India under the Companies Act, 2013, with no extension to LLPs (Indian or foreign) or to companies incorporated outside India
options.C: 'Body corporate' includes every co-operative society and corporation sole registered under any law, since these are treated as functionally equivalent to companies for LLP Act purposes
options.D: It includes: (i) a LLP registered under this Act; (ii) a LLP incorporated outside India; and (iii) a company incorporated outside India; it does NOT include: (i) a corporation sole; (ii) a co-operative society registered under any law for the time being in force; and (iii) any other body corporate (not being a section 2(20) company or an LLP as defined in this Act) which the Central Government may, by notification, specify - and it also does not include Government

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It includes: (i) a LLP registered under this Act; (ii) a LLP incorporated outside India; and (iii) a company incorporated outside India; it does NOT include: (i) a corporation sole; (ii) a co-operative society registered under any law for the time being in force; and (iii) any other body corporate (not being a section 2(20) company or an LLP as defined in this Act) which the Central Government may, by notification, specify - and it also does not include Government

Section 2(1)(d) builds an inclusive/exclusive definition around the Companies Act's own 'company' definition - it deliberately pulls in Indian and foreign LLPs and foreign companies, while carving out corporation soles, co-operative societies, CG-notified other bodies, and the Government itself.

question_html: Under section 2(1)(k), what does 'entity' mean generally, and for which specific sections is this meaning extended to also include a firm set up under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932?

options.A: 'Entity' generally means any body corporate; however, for the purposes of sections 18, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52 and 53 specifically, 'entity' is extended to also include a firm set up under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
options.B: 'Entity' means any body corporate universally throughout the LLP Act, with no provision anywhere extending its meaning to include a traditional partnership firm under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
options.C: 'Entity' is defined to mean exclusively a firm set up under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, with body corporates being entirely excluded from this definition under section 2(1)(k)
options.D: The extended meaning of 'entity' (including a partnership firm) applies universally across every section of the LLP Act, 2008, not merely to the specific sections listed in section 2(1)(k)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) 'Entity' generally means any body corporate; however, for the purposes of sections 18, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52 and 53 specifically, 'entity' is extended to also include a firm set up under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932

Section 2(1)(k) is a general body-corporate definition with a narrow, section-specific extension - only within the particular sections enumerated (18, 46-50, 52, 53) does 'entity' additionally sweep in a traditional Indian Partnership Act firm, a deliberate drafting choice to keep the general definition clean while enabling those specific provisions to also reach firms.

question_html: Under section 2(1)(m), what does 'Foreign LLP' mean?

options.A: 'Foreign LLP' means any LLP formed, incorporated, or registered outside India, regardless of whether it establishes any place of business within India or has any connection to India whatsoever
options.B: 'Foreign LLP' means a LLP formed, incorporated, or registered outside India which establishes a place of business within India
options.C: 'Foreign LLP' means an Indian-registered LLP that has established a place of business outside India, i.e., the reverse of the actual statutory meaning
options.D: 'Foreign LLP' means a body corporate incorporated outside India that conducts business exclusively through electronic mode, with no requirement of any physical place of business anywhere

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) 'Foreign LLP' means a LLP formed, incorporated, or registered outside India which establishes a place of business within India

Section 2(1)(m) mirrors the two-limb foreign-entity structure seen elsewhere in company law - a 'Foreign LLP' must both be formed/incorporated/registered outside India AND have established a place of business within India; formation abroad alone, without an Indian place of business, does not suffice.

question_html: What is the default meaning of 'financial year' for an LLP, and what special rule applies where an LLP is incorporated after 30th September of a year? What is the outer cap on the period for which the first accounts of an LLP may be prepared?

options.A: 'Financial year' always means the calendar year (1st January to 31st December), with no special rule for LLPs incorporated after 30th September, and the first-accounts period may extend up to 24 months without restriction
options.B: Where an LLP is incorporated after 30th September, its financial year must end on 31st March of that SAME year (i.e., within just a few months), rather than being permitted to extend into the following year
options.C: 'Financial year' means the period from 1st April of a year to 31st March of the following year; however, where the LLP is incorporated AFTER 30th September of a year, the financial year may end on 31st March of the year NEXT following that year; in all cases, the period for which the first accounts of the LLP are prepared shall not exceed 18 months
options.D: There is no statutory cap on the period for which an LLP's first accounts may be prepared; an LLP may defer its first accounts indefinitely until it chooses to close its books

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 'Financial year' means the period from 1st April of a year to 31st March of the following year; however, where the LLP is incorporated AFTER 30th September of a year, the financial year may end on 31st March of the year NEXT following that year; in all cases, the period for which the first accounts of the LLP are prepared shall not exceed 18 months

The default 1st April-31st March financial year gets a special extension for LLPs incorporated late in a fiscal year (after 30th September) - their first financial year may run through to 31st March of the FOLLOWING year rather than being cut short - but the outer statutory limit on the first-accounts period remains 18 months regardless.

question_html: Under section 2(1)(ta), what are the contribution and turnover thresholds (and their respective prescribable upper caps) that qualify a limited liability partnership as a 'Small LLP'?

options.A: The contribution threshold is Rs. 40 lakh (uncapped upward) and the turnover threshold is Rs. 25 lakh (capped at Rs. 5 crore) - the reverse of the actual statutory allocation between the two criteria
options.B: A 'Small LLP' is defined solely by the number of partners (not exceeding 5), with no reference whatsoever to contribution or turnover figures
options.C: Both the contribution and turnover thresholds are fixed, immutable figures (Rs. 25 lakh and Rs. 40 lakh respectively) with no statutory provision allowing the Central Government to prescribe any higher amount
options.D: An LLP qualifies as a 'Small LLP' if its contribution does not exceed Rs. 25 lakh (or such higher amount, not exceeding Rs. 5 crore, as may be prescribed), and its turnover (as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year) does not exceed Rs. 40 lakh (or such higher amount, not exceeding Rs. 50 crore, as may be prescribed), or it meets such other prescribed requirements and conditions

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) An LLP qualifies as a 'Small LLP' if its contribution does not exceed Rs. 25 lakh (or such higher amount, not exceeding Rs. 5 crore, as may be prescribed), and its turnover (as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year) does not exceed Rs. 40 lakh (or such higher amount, not exceeding Rs. 50 crore, as may be prescribed), or it meets such other prescribed requirements and conditions

Section 2(1)(ta) sets a base contribution threshold of Rs. 25 lakh (prescribable up to Rs. 5 crore) and a base turnover threshold of Rs. 40 lakh, measured against the immediately preceding financial year's Statement of Account and Solvency (prescribable up to Rs. 50 crore) - both figures carry statutory headroom for the Central Government to raise them by prescription.

question_html: An LLP is incorporated on 15th October, 2022. Over what maximum period may its financial year run, and may the LLP instead choose to prepare its first accounts for a shorter period?

question_html: Under section 3, what effect does the death, insanity, retirement, or insolvency of a partner have on the existence of the LLP, and what capacities does perpetual succession give the LLP?

options.A: The LLP is automatically dissolved upon the death, insanity, retirement, or insolvency of ANY partner, requiring fresh incorporation with the remaining partners if the business is to continue
options.B: None of these events (death, insanity, retirement, or insolvency of a partner) affects the existence, rights, or liabilities of the LLP; the LLP continues its existence irrespective of changes in its partners, and, by virtue of perpetual succession, is capable of entering into contracts and holding property in its own name
options.C: Perpetual succession applies only where the departing partner is a designated partner; the death, insanity, retirement, or insolvency of a non-designated partner does cause automatic dissolution of the LLP
options.D: The LLP continues to exist after a partner's death or insolvency, but loses its capacity to enter into new contracts or hold property until a replacement partner is formally appointed

question_html: As a separate legal entity, to what extent is the LLP itself liable for its obligations, to what extent is a partner's liability limited, and against whom may the LLP's creditors proceed?

options.A: The LLP's separate legal entity status means creditors of the LLP automatically become creditors of each individual partner as well, entitling them to pursue the partners' personal assets without limit
options.B: As a separate legal entity, the LLP bears no liability of its own whatsoever; all obligations pass through directly and exclusively to the partners in their personal capacity
options.C: The LLP is liable to the full extent of its assets, but the liability of the partners is limited to their agreed contribution in the LLP; creditors of the LLP are the creditors of the LLP ALONE - in other words, they cannot look to the partners' personal assets beyond the agreed contribution
options.D: The LLP's liability is capped at the aggregate agreed contribution of all partners combined, with any liability beyond that amount simply extinguished and unenforceable by creditors

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The LLP is liable to the full extent of its assets, but the liability of the partners is limited to their agreed contribution in the LLP; creditors of the LLP are the creditors of the LLP ALONE - in other words, they cannot look to the partners' personal assets beyond the agreed contribution

This is the practical payoff of separate legal entity status - the LLP's own assets (not the aggregate partner contributions, and not partners' personal wealth) answer for LLP obligations in full, while partners' exposure is capped at their agreed contribution; creditors of the LLP are confined to the LLP itself, not the individual partners.

question_html: What does the 'mutual agency' characteristic of an LLP mean in terms of one partner's liability for another partner's independent or unauthorized actions?

options.A: Each partner acts as the agent of every OTHER partner individually (in addition to being an agent of the LLP), meaning any partner can freely bind his co-partners personally by his own unauthorized acts
options.B: Mutual agency means that all partners are jointly and severally liable for each other's independent and unauthorized actions, exactly as under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, with no shielding effect at all
options.C: Mutual agency applies only to designated partners; non-designated partners can freely bind their co-partners by unauthorized acts without any restriction under the LLP Act, 2008
options.D: No partner is liable on account of the independent or unauthorized actions of other partners - individual partners are shielded from joint liability created by another partner's wrongful business decisions or misconduct; in other words, all partners are agents of the LLP alone, and no one partner can bind another partner by his own acts

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No partner is liable on account of the independent or unauthorized actions of other partners - individual partners are shielded from joint liability created by another partner's wrongful business decisions or misconduct; in other words, all partners are agents of the LLP alone, and no one partner can bind another partner by his own acts

This is a key structural departure from traditional partnership law - in an LLP, a partner is the agent of the LLP itself, not of his fellow partners, so one partner's rogue or unauthorized conduct does not automatically expose the other partners to joint liability the way it would under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

question_html: Is it mandatory for an LLP to have a common seal, and, as an 'artificial legal person', what can an LLP NOT do that a natural person can?

options.A: No - an LLP may have a common seal, if it decides to have one [Section 14(c)]; it is NOT mandatory. As an artificial legal person, an LLP can do everything a natural person can do EXCEPT that it cannot be sent to jail, cannot take an oath, cannot marry or get divorced, and cannot practice a learned profession like Chartered Accountancy or Medicine; it is invisible, intangible, and immortal (dissolved only by law) but not fictitious, because it genuinely exists
options.B: Every LLP is statutorily required to obtain and use a common seal on all its documents, exactly as was historically required of companies, with no option to dispense with one
options.C: As an artificial legal person, an LLP is barred from suing or being sued, since only natural persons possess standing to participate in legal proceedings under the LLP Act, 2008
options.D: An LLP is a 'fictitious' entity in the legal sense, existing only on paper, with no genuine legal existence independent of the fiction created by its registration documents

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - an LLP may have a common seal, if it decides to have one [Section 14(c)]; it is NOT mandatory. As an artificial legal person, an LLP can do everything a natural person can do EXCEPT that it cannot be sent to jail, cannot take an oath, cannot marry or get divorced, and cannot practice a learned profession like Chartered Accountancy or Medicine; it is invisible, intangible, and immortal (dissolved only by law) but not fictitious, because it genuinely exists

Having a common seal is expressly optional under section 14(c) - a deliberate departure from the older company-law norm; and the study material's characterisation of an LLP as an 'artificial legal person' captures both its extensive powers (contracting, holding property, suing/being sued) and its narrow, human-specific incapacities (imprisonment, oaths, marriage, and personally practising a learned profession), while emphasising it is genuinely (not fictitiously) existent.

question_html: What is the statutory minimum number of partners an LLP must have, what is the minimum number and residency requirement for designated partners, and is there any statutory maximum limit on the total number of partners?

options.A: Every LLP must have at least five partners and at least three designated partners, with a statutory maximum cap of fifty partners in total, beyond which the LLP must convert into a public company
options.B: Every LLP shall have at least two partners, and shall also have at least two individuals as designated partners, of whom at least one shall be resident in India; there is NO maximum limit on the number of partners in an LLP
options.C: The minimum number of partners is two, but the maximum is capped at 200 partners, mirroring the maximum-member limit applicable to a private company under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: There is no minimum requirement for partners in an LLP at all; an LLP may validly operate with a single partner indefinitely, without any consequence, so long as it has at least one designated partner

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Every LLP shall have at least two partners, and shall also have at least two individuals as designated partners, of whom at least one shall be resident in India; there is NO maximum limit on the number of partners in an LLP

The LLP Act sets a floor (2 partners minimum, 2 designated partners minimum with at least one India-resident) but deliberately imposes NO ceiling on the total number of partners - a notable contrast with the 200-member cap applicable to private companies under the Companies Act, 2013.

question_html: Can an LLP be formed for a charitable or non-economic purpose, and what power does the Central Government have to investigate an LLP's affairs?

options.A: An LLP may be freely formed for either profit-making or charitable/non-economic purposes, with no restriction under the LLP Act, 2008 favouring one over the other
options.B: The Central Government has no power whatsoever to investigate the affairs of an LLP; investigation of LLPs falls exclusively within the jurisdiction of the National Company Law Tribunal, acting on its own motion
options.C: No - the essential requirement for forming an LLP is carrying on a lawful business with a view to earn profit; an LLP cannot be formed for a charitable or non-economic purpose. Separately, the Central Government has the power to investigate the affairs of an LLP by appointing a competent authority for that purpose
options.D: An LLP formed for a non-economic purpose is valid so long as it is subsequently converted into a section 8-equivalent not-for-profit entity within one year of incorporation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - the essential requirement for forming an LLP is carrying on a lawful business with a view to earn profit; an LLP cannot be formed for a charitable or non-economic purpose. Separately, the Central Government has the power to investigate the affairs of an LLP by appointing a competent authority for that purpose

The LLP form is purpose-restricted to lawful, profit-oriented business (unlike a section 8 company, which the Companies Act permits for charitable objects) - and, mirroring company-law investigative powers, the Central Government retains the authority to investigate an LLP's affairs through an appointed competent authority.

question_html: Under section 5, who generally may be a partner in an LLP, and what three circumstances render an individual incapable of becoming a partner?

options.A: Only individuals (never body corporates) may be partners in an LLP, and there are no statutory disqualifications of any kind restricting which individuals may become partners
options.B: Any individual or body corporate may be a partner, but the only disqualification is being an undischarged insolvent; unsoundness of mind and pending insolvency applications do not disqualify a person under section 5
options.C: Body corporates are disqualified from being partners in an LLP altogether; only natural individuals meeting certain net-worth criteria (not otherwise specified) may become partners

question_html: Under section 6(2), if the number of partners of an LLP falls below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while so reduced, what is the legal consequence for the sole remaining partner?

options.A: The person who is the sole partner of the LLP during the time it carries on business after those six months, and who has knowledge of the fact that it is carrying on business with him alone, shall be personally liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period
options.B: The LLP is automatically and immediately dissolved the moment its partner count falls below two, with no six-month grace period and no personal liability consequence for the remaining partner
options.C: The sole remaining partner faces no personal liability consequence whatsoever, regardless of how long the LLP continues to carry on business with only one partner, so long as he eventually appoints a second partner

question_html: What is the general minimum requirement for designated partners under section 7(1), and what special rule applies where all the partners of an LLP are bodies corporate, or where some partners are individuals and some are bodies corporate?

options.A: The minimum designated-partner requirement applies only to LLPs with exclusively individual partners; LLPs whose partners are entirely bodies corporate are wholly exempt from having any designated partners at all
options.B: Where all partners are bodies corporate, the bodies corporate themselves (rather than any individual or nominee) must directly act as the designated partners, since only a body corporate can represent another body corporate under section 7(1)
options.C: Every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals, and at least one of them shall be resident in India; however, if all the partners in the LLP are bodies corporate, or if some partners are individuals and some are bodies corporate, then at least two individuals who are partners of such LLP, or nominees of such bodies corporate, shall act as designated partners
options.D: The residency requirement (at least one designated partner resident in India) applies only where the LLP has fewer than five total partners; larger LLPs are exempt from any residency requirement for designated partners

Correct answer: (C) Every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals, and at least one of them shall be resident in India; however, if all the partners in the LLP are bodies corporate, or if some partners are individuals and some are bodies corporate, then at least two individuals who are partners of such LLP, or nominees of such bodies corporate, shall act as designated partners

options.A: No prior consent is required from an individual before he becomes a designated partner; the LLP may unilaterally designate any partner without that partner's knowledge or agreement
options.B: The LLP must file the consenting individual's particulars with the Registrar within 60 days (not 30 days) of his appointment, and no DPIN or equivalent identification number is required under the LLP Act, 2008
options.C: The DPIN requirement applies only to the FIRST designated partner appointed at incorporation; subsequently appointed designated partners are exempt from obtaining any identification number
options.D: An individual shall not become a designated partner in any LLP unless he has given his prior consent to act as such, in the prescribed form and manner; every LLP shall file with the Registrar the particulars of every individual who has given such consent, within 30 days of his appointment; every designated partner of the LLP shall obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number (DPIN) from the Central Government, with sections 153 to 159 of the Companies Act, 2013 applying mutatis mutandis for this purpose

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) An individual shall not become a designated partner in any LLP unless he has given his prior consent to act as such, in the prescribed form and manner; every LLP shall file with the Registrar the particulars of every individual who has given such consent, within 30 days of his appointment; every designated partner of the LLP shall obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number (DPIN) from the Central Government, with sections 153 to 159 of the Companies Act, 2013 applying mutatis mutandis for this purpose

question_html: Under section 7(2), how may the incorporation document itself determine who the designated partners are, and how else may a partner become (or cease to be) a designated partner?

options.A: If the incorporation document specifies who are to be designated partners, such persons shall be designated partners on incorporation; if it instead states that each partner from time to time of the LLP is to be a designated partner, then every partner shall be a designated partner; separately, any partner may become a designated partner by and in accordance with the LLP agreement, and a partner may cease to be a designated partner in accordance with the LLP agreement as well
options.B: The incorporation document can never determine who the designated partners are; designated-partner status can only ever be conferred subsequently, through a separate application filed after incorporation is complete
options.C: Once a person is named a designated partner in the incorporation document, that status is permanent and can never be altered or ended by any subsequent LLP agreement provision
options.D: A partner may become a designated partner only through a fresh incorporation document amendment filed with the Registrar; the LLP agreement has no role whatsoever in conferring or ending designated-partner status

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) If the incorporation document specifies who are to be designated partners, such persons shall be designated partners on incorporation; if it instead states that each partner from time to time of the LLP is to be a designated partner, then every partner shall be a designated partner; separately, any partner may become a designated partner by and in accordance with the LLP agreement, and a partner may cease to be a designated partner in accordance with the LLP agreement as well

Section 7(2) gives two express incorporation-document routes to designated-partner status (naming specific persons, or declaring that every partner from time to time is a designated partner), plus an ongoing LLP-agreement-based route allowing partners to become or cease being designated partners as the agreement provides - a flexible, multi-channel mechanism rather than a single rigid process.

options.A: A designated partner is responsible only for the LLP's day-to-day commercial/business decisions, and bears no liability whatsoever for statutory compliance filings or for penalties imposed on the LLP

question_html: Within what period may an LLP appoint a designated partner to fill a vacancy, and what happens if NO designated partner is appointed, or if at any time there is only ONE designated partner?

options.A: An LLP has 90 days (not 30 days) to fill a designated-partner vacancy, and if no designated partner is appointed within that period, the LLP is automatically and immediately dissolved by operation of law
options.B: If no designated partner is appointed, or there is only one, the Registrar (rather than every partner) is deemed to act as the designated partner until a proper appointment is made
options.C: An LLP may appoint a designated partner within 30 days of a vacancy arising for any reason (with sections 7(4) and 7(5) applying to the new designated partner); however, if no designated partner is appointed, or if at any time there is only one designated partner, EACH PARTNER shall be deemed to be a designated partner
options.D: The 30-day vacancy-filling window applies only to the FIRST vacancy that ever arises in an LLP's existence; subsequent vacancies carry no statutory timeline at all

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) An LLP may appoint a designated partner within 30 days of a vacancy arising for any reason (with sections 7(4) and 7(5) applying to the new designated partner); however, if no designated partner is appointed, or if at any time there is only one designated partner, EACH PARTNER shall be deemed to be a designated partner

question_html: Once the section 11(1)(b) and (c) requirements have been complied with, within what period must the Registrar register the incorporation document and issue a certificate of incorporation, and what evidentiary weight does that certificate carry?

options.A: The Registrar has 60 days (not 14 days) to register the incorporation document, and the resulting certificate is merely PRIMA FACIE (rebuttable) evidence of incorporation, capable of being challenged and overturned in ordinary civil proceedings
options.B: The certificate of incorporation need not be signed by the Registrar at all; a mere electronic acknowledgment of filing, with no official seal or signature, suffices as conclusive evidence of incorporation
options.C: The Registrar's 14-day timeline applies only where section 11(1)(a) has ALSO been complied with; the Registrar may accept the section 11(1)(c) statement in lieu of independently verifying compliance with section 11(1)(a)
options.D: The Registrar shall, within a period of 14 days, register the incorporation document and give a certificate that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified therein; the certificate, signed by the Registrar and authenticated by his official seal, shall be CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified therein

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The Registrar shall, within a period of 14 days, register the incorporation document and give a certificate that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified therein; the certificate, signed by the Registrar and authenticated by his official seal, shall be CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified therein

question_html: To what address may documents be served on an LLP, and when does a change in the LLP's registered office take legal effect?

options.A: The Registrar may reserve the name for a period of 3 months from the date of intimation by the Registrar, provided he is satisfied that the name is not liable to rejection on any ground referred to in section 15(2)
options.B: The Registrar may reserve the name for a period of 12 months from the date of the application, regardless of when the Registrar actually intimates the applicant of the reservation

question_html: If an LLP is, through inadvertence or otherwise, registered by a name identical with or too nearly resembling another LLP, a company, or a registered trademark, within what period may the Central Government direct the LLP to change its name, and within what period may the proprietor of a registered trademark make an application under this section?

options.A: Both the CG's name-change direction period and the trademark proprietor's application window are set at 3 months, with no distinction drawn between the two timelines
options.B: The Central Government may direct the LLP to change its name (or new name) within a period of 3 months from the date of issue of such direction; separately, an application by the proprietor of the registered trademark is maintainable within a period of 3 YEARS from the date of incorporation, registration, or change of name of the LLP under this Act
options.C: The CG's direction period is 3 years (not 3 months), while the trademark proprietor's application window is only 3 months (not 3 years) - the reverse of the actual statutory allocation
options.D: The trademark proprietor has an unlimited, perpetual window within which to apply under section 17, with no outer time limit of any kind

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The Central Government may direct the LLP to change its name (or new name) within a period of 3 months from the date of issue of such direction; separately, an application by the proprietor of the registered trademark is maintainable within a period of 3 YEARS from the date of incorporation, registration, or change of name of the LLP under this Act

question_html: If an LLP defaults in complying with a direction given under section 17(1) to change its name, what happens?

options.A: The LLP is automatically and compulsorily wound up by the Tribunal for failing to comply with the Central Government's name-change direction, with no alternative remedy available
options.B: No consequence follows from non-compliance; the Central Government's direction under section 17(1) is purely advisory and carries no enforcement mechanism whatsoever
options.C: The Central Government shall allot a new name to the LLP, and the Registrar shall enter the new name in the register of LLPs in place of the old name and issue a fresh certificate of incorporation with the new name; this does not, however, prevent the LLP from subsequently changing its name again on its own initiative
options.D: The LLP's registration is permanently cancelled and it ceases to be a body corporate, though its partners may continue operating the business informally as an unregistered partnership firm

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The Central Government shall allot a new name to the LLP, and the Registrar shall enter the new name in the register of LLPs in place of the old name and issue a fresh certificate of incorporation with the new name; this does not, however, prevent the LLP from subsequently changing its name again on its own initiative

Section 17(3) provides a self-executing enforcement mechanism for non-compliance - rather than leaving the LLP nameless or dissolving it, the Central Government simply allots a substitute name, which the Registrar records with a fresh certificate of incorporation, while preserving the LLP's own future freedom to change its name again.

options.A: The penalty is imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, with no fine component at all, mirroring the false-declaration penalty under section 11(3)
options.B: The penalty is a flat fine of Rs. 10,000, with no minimum-maximum range and no possibility of the fine extending beyond that fixed figure
options.C: There is no specific penalty prescribed under section 20 for improper use of 'LLP' or 'Limited Liability Partnership'; such misuse is addressed only through a civil injunction suit brought by an aggrieved LLP
options.D: That person or each of those persons shall be punishable with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh

question_html: Under section 22, who becomes a partner of an LLP on its incorporation, and how may any other person become a partner thereafter? Separately, under section 23(3), can a pre-incorporation written agreement impose obligations on the LLP, and if so, subject to what condition?

options.A: On incorporation of an LLP, the persons who subscribed their names to the incorporation document shall be its partners; any other person may become a partner of the LLP by and in accordance with the LLP agreement. An agreement in writing made before incorporation, between the persons who subscribe their names to the incorporation document, may impose obligations on the LLP - PROVIDED such agreement is ratified by all the partners after the LLP's incorporation
options.B: Only persons expressly nominated by the Registrar (not the subscribers to the incorporation document) become partners on incorporation, and pre-incorporation agreements can never impose any obligation on the LLP under any circumstance, ratified or not
options.C: Every subsequent partner must also personally subscribe to a fresh incorporation document; the LLP agreement route for admitting new partners does not exist under section 22
options.D: A pre-incorporation agreement automatically and unconditionally binds the LLP upon incorporation, with no ratification requirement of any kind under section 23(3)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) On incorporation of an LLP, the persons who subscribed their names to the incorporation document shall be its partners; any other person may become a partner of the LLP by and in accordance with the LLP agreement. An agreement in writing made before incorporation, between the persons who subscribe their names to the incorporation document, may impose obligations on the LLP - PROVIDED such agreement is ratified by all the partners after the LLP's incorporation

Section 22 identifies incorporation-document subscribers as the LLP's original partners, with the LLP agreement governing subsequent admissions, while section 23(3) allows pre-incorporation agreements to bind the LLP only once ratified by all partners after incorporation - preventing an LLP from being saddled with obligations it never truly agreed to.

question_html: Absent any agreement with the other partners as to cessation, what notice period must a resigning partner give, and what three events cause a person to automatically cease to be a partner regardless of any agreement?

options.A: The default notice period for resignation is 90 days (not 30 days), and cessation occurs automatically only upon a partner's death - unsoundness of mind and insolvency-related events do NOT cause automatic cessation under section 24(1)/(2)
options.B: In the absence of an agreement with the other partners as to cessation, a person may resign by giving not less than 30 days' written notice of his intention to resign to the other partners; a person shall automatically cease to be a partner (a) on his death or dissolution of the LLP; (b) if he is declared to be of unsound mind by a competent court; or (c) if he has applied to be adjudged as an insolvent, or has been declared insolvent

options.D: The 30-day notice requirement applies universally, even where the partners have their own agreed cessation mechanism; section 24 overrides any contrary agreement between the partners

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) In the absence of an agreement with the other partners as to cessation, a person may resign by giving not less than 30 days' written notice of his intention to resign to the other partners; a person shall automatically cease to be a partner (a) on his death or dissolution of the LLP; (b) if he is declared to be of unsound mind by a competent court; or (c) if he has applied to be adjudged as an insolvent, or has been declared insolvent

question_html: What is a former partner (or a person entitled to his share) generally entitled to receive from the LLP on cessation, and under what circumstance is a former partner still treated as a partner in relation to persons dealing with the LLP?

options.A: A former partner is entitled to receive a fixed statutory amount of Rs. 1 lakh from the LLP regardless of his actual capital contribution or share of accumulated profits, and retains full management-interference rights even after ceasing to be a partner
options.B: A former partner is deemed to still be a partner in relation to third parties dealing with the LLP ONLY if he personally continues attending LLP meetings; mere absence of notice to the Registrar or to the dealing party is irrelevant
options.C: Unless otherwise provided in the LLP agreement, the former partner (or a person entitled to his share due to his death or insolvency) is entitled to receive from the LLP an amount equal to his actual capital contribution, plus his right to share in the LLP's accumulated profits (after deducting accumulated losses), determined as at the date he ceased to be a partner - but he has no right to interfere in the LLP's management; separately, a former partner continues to be REGARDED as still being a partner (in relation to any person dealing with the LLP) unless that person has notice of the cessation, OR notice of the cessation has been delivered to the Registrar
options.D: A former partner forfeits his entire capital contribution and any share of accumulated profits upon cessation, receiving nothing further from the LLP under any circumstance

question_html: Within what period must a partner inform the LLP of a change in his name or address, and within what period must the LLP file a notice with the Registrar (a) where a person becomes or ceases to be a partner, and (b) where there is a change in a partner's name or address?

options.A: The partner has 30 days to inform the LLP, while the LLP has only 15 days to file the corresponding notice with the Registrar - the reverse of the actual statutory timelines
options.B: Both the partner's duty to inform the LLP and the LLP's duty to file with the Registrar carry a uniform 60-day period, with no distinction between the two obligations
options.C: There is no statutory timeline for either the partner informing the LLP or the LLP filing with the Registrar; both are left entirely to the LLP agreement's discretion under section 25
options.D: Every partner shall inform the LLP of any change in his name or address within a period of 15 days of such change; the LLP shall file a notice with the Registrar within 30 days from the date a person becomes or ceases to be a partner, and also within 30 days of any change in the name or address of a partner

Correct answer: (D) Every partner shall inform the LLP of any change in his name or address within a period of 15 days of such change; the LLP shall file a notice with the Registrar within 30 days from the date a person becomes or ceases to be a partner, and also within 30 days of any change in the name or address of a partner

question_html: Under section 25(3), what form/fee requirements apply to the notice filed with the Registrar, who must sign it, and what must the notice additionally contain if it relates to an incoming partner?

options.A: The notice shall be in the prescribed form, accompanied by prescribed fees, and signed by the designated partner of the LLP and authenticated in the prescribed manner; if the notice relates to an incoming partner, it shall additionally contain a statement by that incoming partner that he consents to becoming a partner, signed by him and authenticated as prescribed
options.B: The notice may be signed by ANY partner (not specifically a designated partner), and no consent statement from an incoming partner is required to accompany a notice of his admission
options.C: The notice is exempt from any prescribed form or fee requirement; a simple, unsigned letter to the Registrar suffices to satisfy section 25(3) in every case
options.D: The consent-statement requirement for incoming partners applies only where the incoming partner is also simultaneously being appointed as a designated partner; ordinary incoming partners need not provide any consent statement

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The notice shall be in the prescribed form, accompanied by prescribed fees, and signed by the designated partner of the LLP and authenticated in the prescribed manner; if the notice relates to an incoming partner, it shall additionally contain a statement by that incoming partner that he consents to becoming a partner, signed by him and authenticated as prescribed

question_html: If a person who has ceased to be a partner has reasonable cause to believe the LLP may not file the required notice with the Registrar, what may he do himself, and what happens if the LLP gives no confirmation within 15 days?

options.A: A departing partner has no independent right to file any notice himself; he must wait indefinitely for the LLP to file the notice, however long that takes, with no self-help remedy available under section 25
options.B: Such a person may himself file with the Registrar the notice referred to in section 25(3); the Registrar shall then obtain confirmation of this from the LLP, unless the LLP has also filed such a notice itself - and where NO confirmation is given by the LLP within 15 days, the Registrar shall register the notice made by the person ceasing to be a partner
options.C: If the LLP gives no confirmation within 15 days, the Registrar must REJECT the departing partner's self-filed notice outright, treating the LLP's silence as an implicit denial of the cessation
options.D: A departing partner may file the notice himself only with the prior written consent of all the other remaining partners of the LLP, defeating the self-help purpose of section 25(6)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Such a person may himself file with the Registrar the notice referred to in section 25(3); the Registrar shall then obtain confirmation of this from the LLP, unless the LLP has also filed such a notice itself - and where NO confirmation is given by the LLP within 15 days, the Registrar shall register the notice made by the person ceasing to be a partner

Section 25(6) gives a departing partner a practical self-help remedy against a potentially uncooperative LLP - he may file the cessation notice himself, and if the LLP fails to confirm (or itself file) within 15 days, the Registrar proceeds to register the partner's own notice, ensuring the cessation gets properly recorded even without the LLP's active cooperation.

question_html: Under section 27(1), when is an LLP NOT bound by something done by a partner in dealing with a third person? Under section 27(2), when IS the LLP liable in respect of a partner's conduct?

options.A: The LLP is never bound by a partner's acts under any circumstance, even where the partner has full actual authority and the third party reasonably believed him to be a partner acting for the LLP
options.B: The LLP is bound by EVERY act of a partner regardless of authority or the third party's knowledge, since section 27(1) imposes no conditions at all on when the LLP escapes liability
options.C: The LLP is not bound by a partner's act if (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP in doing that particular act, AND (b) the person he is dealing with knows he has no such authority, or does not know or believe him to be a partner of the LLP; conversely, the LLP IS liable if a partner is liable to any person as a result of a wrongful act or omission on his part in the course of the LLP's business, or with its authority
options.D: The LLP is liable for a partner's wrongful act or omission only if that act occurred entirely OUTSIDE the course of LLP business and without any LLP authority, the reverse of the actual section 27(2) test

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The LLP is not bound by a partner's act if (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP in doing that particular act, AND (b) the person he is dealing with knows he has no such authority, or does not know or believe him to be a partner of the LLP; conversely, the LLP IS liable if a partner is liable to any person as a result of a wrongful act or omission on his part in the course of the LLP's business, or with its authority

Section 27(1)'s two-part conjunctive test (no actual authority AND the third party's lack of knowledge/belief) protects the LLP from unauthorised acts only where the counterparty isn't reasonably misled, while section 27(2) makes the LLP answerable for a partner's wrongful acts or omissions committed in the course of, or with the authority of, the LLP's business - obligations that, per section 27(3)/(4), remain solely the LLP's own and are met from LLP property.

question_html: Under section 28, is a partner personally liable for an obligation of the LLP solely by reason of being a partner? Is he personally liable for his OWN wrongful act or omission, and for another partner's wrongful act or omission?

options.A: A partner is fully and personally liable for every obligation of the LLP simply by virtue of being a partner, exactly as under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, with no limited-liability protection at all
options.B: A partner is personally liable for other partners' wrongful acts and omissions, but is expressly IMMUNE from personal liability for his own wrongful acts or omissions - the reverse of the actual section 28(2) rule
options.C: Section 28 abolishes all forms of partner liability whatsoever, including liability for a partner's own deliberate wrongful conduct carried out in the course of LLP business
options.D: A partner is NOT personally liable, directly or indirectly, for an LLP obligation solely by reason of being a partner; however, this does not affect a partner's personal liability for his OWN wrongful act or omission - though a partner shall NOT be personally liable for the wrongful act or omission of any OTHER partner of the LLP

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A partner is NOT personally liable, directly or indirectly, for an LLP obligation solely by reason of being a partner; however, this does not affect a partner's personal liability for his OWN wrongful act or omission - though a partner shall NOT be personally liable for the wrongful act or omission of any OTHER partner of the LLP

Section 28 crystallises the LLP's core liability-shield promise - mere partnership status does not expose a partner to the LLP's general obligations - while carefully preserving personal accountability for one's OWN wrongful acts or omissions, and equally carefully NOT extending that personal liability to a partner's co-partners' wrongful conduct.

question_html: If a person, by words or conduct, represents himself (or knowingly permits himself to be represented) as a partner in an LLP, and someone extends credit to the LLP on the faith of that representation, who is liable, and to what extent is the LLP itself liable?

options.A: That person is liable to anyone who, on the faith of the representation, gave credit to the LLP - regardless of whether he knew the representation had reached the person giving credit; where the LLP actually receives credit as a result of such representation, the LLP itself (without prejudice to the representing person's own liability) is liable to the extent of the credit received, or any financial benefit derived from it
options.B: Only the LLP is liable in a holding-out scenario; the individual who falsely represented himself as a partner bears no personal liability whatsoever to the person who extended credit
options.C: The person representing himself as a partner is liable only if he KNEW his representation had actually reached the person extending credit; if he was unaware the representation had reached that person, he bears no liability at all
options.D: The LLP bears no liability at all in a holding-out scenario, even where it directly benefited from and retained the credit extended on the faith of the false representation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) That person is liable to anyone who, on the faith of the representation, gave credit to the LLP - regardless of whether he knew the representation had reached the person giving credit; where the LLP actually receives credit as a result of such representation, the LLP itself (without prejudice to the representing person's own liability) is liable to the extent of the credit received, or any financial benefit derived from it

Section 29's holding-out doctrine protects third parties who reasonably relied on a false partner-representation - the representing individual is liable regardless of whether he knew his representation reached the credit-giver, and the LLP, where it actually received credit or benefit from that representation, is separately liable to the extent of what it received - a dual-liability structure protecting the relying creditor.

question_html: If an act is carried out by an LLP, or any of its partners, with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, what happens to the liability of the LLP and the fraudulently-acting partners? If the fraudulent act was carried out by a PARTNER, on what basis can the LLP avoid being held liable to the same extent as that partner?

options.A: The LLP's liability remains limited to the agreed contribution of its partners even in cases of proven fraud, with unlimited liability applying only to the individual fraudulent partner and never to the LLP itself
options.B: The liability of the LLP, and of the partners who acted with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, shall be UNLIMITED for all or any of the debts or other liabilities of the LLP; however, where such an act is carried out by a partner, the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner UNLESS the LLP establishes that the act was carried out without the LLP's knowledge or authority
options.C: The LLP automatically escapes all liability for a partner's fraudulent act, with no burden on the LLP to establish lack of knowledge or authority - the burden instead falls entirely on the defrauded creditor to prove the LLP's complicity
options.D: Unlimited liability under section 30(1) applies only to designated partners who commit fraud; ordinary (non-designated) partners retain limited liability even where they personally acted with fraudulent intent

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The liability of the LLP, and of the partners who acted with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, shall be UNLIMITED for all or any of the debts or other liabilities of the LLP; however, where such an act is carried out by a partner, the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner UNLESS the LLP establishes that the act was carried out without the LLP's knowledge or authority

Section 30(1) is the LLP Act's key fraud exception to limited liability - both the LLP and the fraudulently-acting partner(s) face unlimited exposure, and where a partner (not the LLP itself) commits the fraud, the LLP shares that unlimited exposure UNLESS it affirmatively proves the act was done without its knowledge or authority - placing the burden of proof on the LLP.

question_html: What punishment does a person who was knowingly a party to carrying on the LLP's business with fraudulent intent face under section 30(2)? Separately, under section 30(3), what is the LLP's compensation liability where its affairs have been conducted fraudulently, and when is the LLP relieved of that liability?

options.A: The punishment under section 30(2) is a fine only (no imprisonment component), and the LLP under section 30(3) is liable to pay compensation in every case, with no knowledge-based exception available to it
options.B: The maximum imprisonment term under section 30(2) is 10 years (not 5 years), and the compensation liability under section 30(3) attaches only to the fraudulent individual, never to the LLP itself
options.C: Under section 30(2), such a person is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 5 years, and with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh; under section 30(3), where the LLP's affairs (through a partner, designated partner, or employee) have been conducted fraudulently, the LLP and that person are liable to pay compensation to anyone suffering loss/damage - but the LLP is NOT liable if the fraudulent act was committed WITHOUT the LLP's knowledge
options.D: Section 30(2) applies only to designated partners (not ordinary partners or employees), and section 30(3)'s compensation liability requires a separate criminal conviction before it can arise

Correct answer: (C) Under section 30(2), such a person is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 5 years, and with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh; under section 30(3), where the LLP's affairs (through a partner, designated partner, or employee) have been conducted fraudulently, the LLP and that person are liable to pay compensation to anyone suffering loss/damage - but the LLP is NOT liable if the fraudulent act was committed WITHOUT the LLP's knowledge

question_html: Under section 31, on what basis may a Court or Tribunal reduce or waive a penalty leviable against a partner or employee of an LLP, and what protection is given to a partner or employee who provides such information?

options.A: The Court or Tribunal has no power to reduce or waive penalties under any circumstance, however useful the information provided by a whistle-blowing partner or employee may be
options.B: Whistle-blower protection under section 31(2) applies only to designated partners; ordinary partners and employees who provide useful information receive no protection against discharge, demotion, or harassment
options.C: The penalty-reduction power under section 31(1) applies only where the whistle-blower's information is provided strictly DURING a formal investigation; information volunteered outside an investigation carries no benefit whatsoever
options.D: The Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive a penalty if satisfied that the partner or employee has provided useful information during investigation of the LLP, or that information given by him (whether or not during investigation) has led to the LLP or any partner/employee being convicted under the LLP Act or any other Act; separately, no partner or employee may be discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed, or otherwise discriminated against merely because he provided (or caused to be provided) such information

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive a penalty if satisfied that the partner or employee has provided useful information during investigation of the LLP, or that information given by him (whether or not during investigation) has led to the LLP or any partner/employee being convicted under the LLP Act or any other Act; separately, no partner or employee may be discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed, or otherwise discriminated against merely because he provided (or caused to be provided) such information

Section 31 combines an incentive (discretionary penalty reduction/waiver for useful information, whether given during an investigation or otherwise, so long as it leads to a conviction) with a shield (protection against retaliatory discharge, demotion, suspension, threats, or harassment) - encouraging partners and employees to come forward without fear of reprisal.

question_html: Under section 32, what may a partner's contribution to the LLP consist of, and how must the monetary value of each partner's contribution be treated in the LLP's accounts?

options.A: A partner's contribution may consist of tangible, movable or immovable, or intangible property or other benefit to the LLP, including money, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute cash or property, and contracts for services performed or to be performed; the monetary value of each partner's contribution shall be accounted for and disclosed in the accounts of the LLP in the prescribed manner
options.B: A partner's contribution may consist ONLY of money (cash); property, promissory notes, service contracts, and other benefits are not recognised as valid forms of contribution under section 32
options.C: The monetary value of a partner's contribution need not be accounted for or disclosed anywhere in the LLP's accounts, since contributions are treated as a purely private matter between the partners
options.D: Only tangible, movable property qualifies as a valid contribution under section 32; intangible property, service contracts, and promissory notes are expressly excluded from the definition

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A partner's contribution may consist of tangible, movable or immovable, or intangible property or other benefit to the LLP, including money, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute cash or property, and contracts for services performed or to be performed; the monetary value of each partner's contribution shall be accounted for and disclosed in the accounts of the LLP in the prescribed manner

Section 32 defines 'contribution' expansively - covering tangible and intangible property, movable and immovable property, money, promissory notes, agreements to contribute, and even service contracts - while requiring the monetary value of each such contribution to be properly accounted for and disclosed in the LLP's accounts in the prescribed manner, ensuring transparency about what each partner has actually brought to the LLP.

question_html: Under section 34(1), on what basis and according to what system must an LLP maintain its books of account, and where must those books be maintained?

options.A: The LLP must maintain its books strictly on accrual basis only (cash basis is not permitted), and according to the single-entry system, maintained at any location of the LLP's choosing rather than specifically at its registered office
options.B: The LLP shall maintain such proper books of account as may be prescribed, relating to its affairs for each year of its existence, on CASH BASIS or ACCRUAL BASIS, and according to the DOUBLE ENTRY system of accounting, and shall maintain the same at its REGISTERED OFFICE for such period as may be prescribed
options.C: Books of account under section 34(1) may be maintained on either cash or accrual basis, but only under the single-entry system, since double-entry bookkeeping is reserved exclusively for companies under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: There is no requirement to maintain books of account at the LLP's registered office specifically; any branch office or the designated partner's personal residence suffices under section 34(1)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The LLP shall maintain such proper books of account as may be prescribed, relating to its affairs for each year of its existence, on CASH BASIS or ACCRUAL BASIS, and according to the DOUBLE ENTRY system of accounting, and shall maintain the same at its REGISTERED OFFICE for such period as may be prescribed

Section 34(1) gives LLPs a choice between cash and accrual basis of accounting (unlike companies, which are confined to accrual basis under the Companies Act) but mandates the double-entry system, with the books required to be kept at the LLP's registered office for the prescribed retention period.

question_html: Within what period after the end of each financial year must an LLP prepare its Statement of Account and Solvency, who must sign it, and does the Central Government have any power to exempt LLPs from the audit requirement?

options.A: The Statement of Account and Solvency must be prepared within 3 months (not 6 months) of the financial year's end, and must be signed by the LLP's statutory auditor rather than by its designated partners
options.B: The Central Government has no power whatsoever to exempt any LLP from the audit requirement; every LLP, without exception, must have its accounts audited under section 34(4)
options.C: Every LLP shall, within a period of 6 months from the end of each financial year, prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency for that financial year, as at the last day of that financial year, in the prescribed form; the statement shall be signed by the designated partners of the LLP; separately, while the LLP's accounts shall generally be audited in accordance with prescribed rules, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exempt any class or classes of LLP from the audit requirement
options.D: The Statement of Account and Solvency need be signed only by ordinary (non-designated) partners; designated partners are expressly excluded from the signing requirement under section 34(2)

Correct answer: (C) Every LLP shall, within a period of 6 months from the end of each financial year, prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency for that financial year, as at the last day of that financial year, in the prescribed form; the statement shall be signed by the designated partners of the LLP; separately, while the LLP's accounts shall generally be audited in accordance with prescribed rules, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exempt any class or classes of LLP from the audit requirement

Section 34(2) sets a 6-month post-financial-year-end preparation deadline for the Statement of Account and Solvency, requiring designated-partner signatures, while section 34(4) preserves general audit compliance but expressly empowers the Central Government to carve out exempted classes of LLP by Gazette notification - a flexibility particularly relevant to smaller LLPs.

options.A: The annual return must be filed within 30 days (not 60 days) of the financial year's closure, and the penalty for non-filing is a flat one-time amount with no daily continuing-default component
options.B: The annual return filing deadline is 6 months from the financial year's closure (matching the Statement of Account and Solvency timeline), rather than the shorter 60-day period actually prescribed under section 35

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Every LLP shall file an annual return, duly authenticated, with the Registrar within 60 days of closure of its financial year; the penalty for non-filing is Rs. 100 per day, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1,00,000 for the LLP, and Rs. 100 per day subject to a maximum of Rs. 50,000 for every designated partner

options.A: The incorporation document, the names of partners and any changes made therein, the Statement of Account and Solvency, and the annual return filed by each LLP with the Registrar shall be available for inspection by any person, in the prescribed manner and on payment of the prescribed fee; a person who makes a statement that is false in any material particular (knowing it to be false) or that omits any material fact (knowing it to be material) shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, and shall also be liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 1 lakh but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh
options.B: Only the incorporation document is available for public inspection under section 36; the Statement of Account and Solvency and the annual return are treated as confidential and are not open to inspection by any person
options.C: The section 37 penalty for a false statement is a fine-only penalty (no imprisonment), and the fine has no prescribed minimum, ranging from Rs. 0 up to Rs. 5 lakh at the adjudicating authority's discretion
options.D: Inspection of Registrar-held LLP documents under section 36 is restricted to Government officials and cannot be accessed by any private citizen or member of the public, however the prescribed fee is paid

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The incorporation document, the names of partners and any changes made therein, the Statement of Account and Solvency, and the annual return filed by each LLP with the Registrar shall be available for inspection by any person, in the prescribed manner and on payment of the prescribed fee; a person who makes a statement that is false in any material particular (knowing it to be false) or that omits any material fact (knowing it to be material) shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, and shall also be liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 1 lakh but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh

Section 36 makes core LLP filings - incorporation document, partner particulars/changes, the Statement of Account and Solvency, and the annual return - publicly inspectable (for a fee), promoting transparency, while section 37 backs the integrity of these filings with a meaningful penalty (up to 2 years' imprisonment plus a Rs. 1 lakh-5 lakh fine) for knowingly false or materially incomplete statements.

question_html: Whom may the Registrar require to answer questions, make declarations, or supply particulars under section 38(1), what power does the Registrar have if such a person does not respond satisfactorily, and what penalty applies to a person who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with a Registrar's summons?

options.A: The Registrar's power to require information is confined to CURRENT partners and designated partners only; former partners, designated partners, and employees are entirely outside the Registrar's power to require information
options.B: The Registrar may require any person, including any present or former partner, designated partner, or employee of an LLP, to answer any question, make any declaration, or supply any details/particulars in writing within a reasonable period; if such a person does not respond satisfactorily (or at all) within a reasonable time, the Registrar has the power to summon that person to appear before him, an inspector, or another designated public officer; a person who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with such a summons or requisition shall be punishable with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 2,000 but which may extend to Rs. 25,000
options.C: Non-compliance with a Registrar's summons under section 38 attracts imprisonment for a term which may extend to 1 year, with no fine component at all, materially different from the actual fine-only penalty structure
options.D: The Registrar has no power to summon a non-responsive person to appear before him or any other officer; his powers under section 38 are limited to receiving voluntary written responses, with no compulsion mechanism available

Correct answer: (B) The Registrar may require any person, including any present or former partner, designated partner, or employee of an LLP, to answer any question, make any declaration, or supply any details/particulars in writing within a reasonable period; if such a person does not respond satisfactorily (or at all) within a reasonable time, the Registrar has the power to summon that person to appear before him, an inspector, or another designated public officer; a person who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with such a summons or requisition shall be punishable with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 2,000 but which may extend to Rs. 25,000

When the Regional Director compounded the March 2025 offence, within what range must the sum collected from Kestrel Innovations LLP have fallen?

options.A: The Regional Director may collect any sum he considers appropriate, with no reference at all to the minimum or maximum fine prescribed for the underlying offence under section 38(3)
options.B: The compounding sum must be exactly equal to the maximum fine prescribed for the offence (Rs. 25,000), with no discretion to collect any lesser amount within the statutory range
options.C: The Regional Director may compound the offence by collecting a sum which may extend to the amount of the maximum fine provided for the offence (Rs. 25,000), but which shall not be lower than the minimum amount provided for the offence (Rs. 2,000) - so the compounding sum must fall between Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 25,000
options.D: The compounding sum must be exactly equal to the minimum fine prescribed for the offence (Rs. 2,000), since section 39(1) requires the Regional Director to always apply the statutory floor rather than a higher amount

Correct answer: (C) The Regional Director may compound the offence by collecting a sum which may extend to the amount of the maximum fine provided for the offence (Rs. 25,000), but which shall not be lower than the minimum amount provided for the offence (Rs. 2,000) - so the compounding sum must fall between Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 25,000

Section 39(1) confines the Regional Director's compounding discretion within the offence's own statutory fine range - here, Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 25,000 under section 38(3) - never below the minimum, never above the maximum.

Can the Regional Director compound Kestrel Innovations LLP's February 2027 offence (a similar offence committed within three years of the March 2025 compounding)?

options.A: Yes - section 39 permits unlimited repeated compounding of similar offences by the same LLP, with no time-based restriction on how frequently an offence may be compounded
options.B: Yes - the three-year bar under section 39(2) applies only to offences committed by INDIVIDUAL partners or designated partners personally; it does not apply where the offence is attributed to the LLP itself
options.C: No - but only because compounding under section 39 is a strictly one-time, lifetime privilege for any LLP, regardless of how much time has elapsed since the first compounding
options.D: No - under section 39(2), the compounding provisions do not apply to an offence committed by an LLP (or its partner/designated partner) within a period of THREE YEARS from the date on which a similar offence committed by it was previously compounded; since the February 2027 offence falls within three years of the March 2025 compounding, it cannot again be compounded

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - under section 39(2), the compounding provisions do not apply to an offence committed by an LLP (or its partner/designated partner) within a period of THREE YEARS from the date on which a similar offence committed by it was previously compounded; since the February 2027 offence falls within three years of the March 2025 compounding, it cannot again be compounded

Section 39(2) imposes a three-year cooling-off bar on re-compounding a similar offence - Kestrel Innovations LLP's February 2027 default falls squarely within three years of its March 2025 compounding, so this second offence cannot be compounded again under section 39; per the Explanation, only a second/subsequent offence committed AFTER the three-year period expires is treated as a fresh 'first offence' eligible for compounding.
