Assuming the March 2025 compounding of Kestrel Innovations LLP's offence occurred BEFORE any prosecution had been instituted in relation to that offence, what is the legal effect under section 39(5)?

options.A: Where an offence is compounded before the institution of any prosecution, no prosecution shall be instituted in relation to that offence
options.B: Compounding before institution of prosecution has no legal effect on whether a prosecution may subsequently be instituted; the Registrar retains full discretion to prosecute regardless of the prior compounding
options.C: Prosecution must still be instituted even after pre-prosecution compounding, but the court is required to acquit the LLP automatically upon proof that compounding had occurred

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Where an offence is compounded before the institution of any prosecution, no prosecution shall be instituted in relation to that offence

Section 39(5) gives pre-prosecution compounding a clean, preventive effect - once the offence has been compounded before any prosecution is instituted, no prosecution may be instituted at all in relation to that offence, sparing the LLP (and the compounding authority) the need for any subsequent court proceeding.

question_html:
Bellhaven Consultants LLP failed to file its Statement of Account and Solvency with the Registrar despite being served a notice by the Registrar requiring it to do so. Separately, one of Bellhaven Consultants LLP's partners, Ms. Farah Sultana, enters into a written assignment transferring 30% of her right to share in the LLP's profits and losses to an outside investor, Mr. Devraj Oberoi, who is not himself admitted as a partner of the LLP.

If Bellhaven Consultants LLP fails to make good its default within 14 days after being served the Registrar's notice, what may the Registrar do, and what power does the Tribunal have under section 41?

options.A: The Registrar has no recourse to the Tribunal at all under section 41; the only remedy for non-filing of the Statement of Account and Solvency is the standalone penalty prescribed under section 34(5)
options.B: The Tribunal may, on application by the Registrar, make an order directing Bellhaven Consultants LLP, or its designated partners, or its partners, to make good the default within such time as specified in the order; any such order may also provide that all costs of and incidental to the application shall be borne by the LLP
options.C: The Tribunal's order under section 41 can only impose a monetary fine on the LLP; it has no power to direct the LLP or its partners/designated partners to actually make good the default itself
options.D: The 14-day cure period under section 41 runs from the ORIGINAL due date for filing the Statement of Account and Solvency, rather than from the date the Registrar's notice requiring compliance is served

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The Tribunal may, on application by the Registrar, make an order directing Bellhaven Consultants LLP, or its designated partners, or its partners, to make good the default within such time as specified in the order; any such order may also provide that all costs of and incidental to the application shall be borne by the LLP

Section 41 gives the Registrar a Tribunal-backed enforcement mechanism distinct from the standalone monetary penalties elsewhere in the Act - after a 14-day post-notice cure period lapses without compliance, the Registrar may apply to the Tribunal, which can order the LLP (or its partners/designated partners) to make good the default within a specified time, with costs of the application potentially borne by the LLP.

At the creditors' meeting convened by Tribunal order, creditors representing 80% in value of those present agree to the proposed compromise.

Since creditors representing 80% in value of those present at the meeting agreed to the compromise, can the Tribunal sanction this compromise and make it binding on ALL of Alderwood Ventures LLP's creditors, including those who did not agree?

options.A: Yes - under section 60(2), if a majority representing THREE-FOURTHS (75%) in value of the creditors at the meeting agree to the compromise, and it is sanctioned by the Tribunal by order, the compromise shall be binding on all the creditors (and on the LLP itself, or on the liquidator and contributories if the LLP is being wound up); since 80% exceeds the 75% threshold, the Tribunal may sanction the compromise, making it binding on all creditors including dissenters
options.B: No - section 60(2) requires UNANIMOUS (100%) agreement of all creditors before the Tribunal can sanction any compromise; an 80% majority, however large, is insufficient to bind dissenting creditors
options.C: No - the 80% agreement is irrelevant because compromises with creditors are governed exclusively by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, not by section 60 of the LLP Act, 2008
options.D: Yes, but only if EVERY creditor who did not attend the meeting is separately and individually notified and consents in writing after the meeting, in addition to the 80% who agreed at the meeting itself

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - under section 60(2), if a majority representing THREE-FOURTHS (75%) in value of the creditors at the meeting agree to the compromise, and it is sanctioned by the Tribunal by order, the compromise shall be binding on all the creditors (and on the LLP itself, or on the liquidator and contributories if the LLP is being wound up); since 80% exceeds the 75% threshold, the Tribunal may sanction the compromise, making it binding on all creditors including dissenters

Section 60(2)'s three-fourths-in-value threshold is the statutory bar for binding dissenting/absent creditors - Alderwood Ventures LLP's 80% agreement clears this bar, so once the Tribunal sanctions the compromise by order, it becomes binding on all creditors, the LLP, and (where relevant) the liquidator and contributories, subject to the Tribunal being satisfied that all material facts (including the LLP's latest financial position and any pending investigations) have been disclosed.

Given that Thornfield Agro LLP's partners were reduced to one and it carried on business for 8 months thereafter, does this by itself constitute an independent ground on which the Tribunal may order the LLP to be wound up?

Correct answer: (B) Yes - under section 64(b), an LLP may be wound up by the Tribunal if, for a period of more than six months, the number of partners of the LLP is reduced below two; Thornfield Agro LLP's 8-month continuation with only one partner exceeds this six-month threshold, making this an independent ground for Tribunal winding up

Section 64(b) stands as an independent, self-sufficient ground for Tribunal winding up - once the partner count has been below two for more than six months, this alone (without needing any additional default, such as a filing failure) empowers the Tribunal to wind up the LLP, distinct from (though factually overlapping with) the personal-liability consequence under section 6(2) for the sole remaining partner.

How does the liability of the owners differ across a partnership firm, an LLP, and a private company?

options.A: In a partnership firm, the liability of each partner is UNLIMITED and can extend to the partners' personal assets; in an LLP, the liability of each partner is LIMITED to the extent of the agreed contribution in the LLP, except in case of willful fraud (where liability becomes unlimited); in a private company, the liability of a member is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares held by them
options.B: Liability is identical across all three structures - limited to the agreed capital contribution in every case - with no distinction between a partnership firm, an LLP, and a private company
options.C: Partnership firm partners enjoy limited liability capped at their capital contribution, while LLP partners and private company members both bear unlimited personal liability for all business obligations
options.D: LLP partners bear unlimited personal liability in every case, identical to partnership firm partners, while only private company members enjoy any form of limited liability

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) In a partnership firm, the liability of each partner is UNLIMITED and can extend to the partners' personal assets; in an LLP, the liability of each partner is LIMITED to the extent of the agreed contribution in the LLP, except in case of willful fraud (where liability becomes unlimited); in a private company, the liability of a member is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares held by them

This is the fundamental structural distinction the three friends must weigh - the partnership firm exposes personal assets without limit, the LLP caps exposure at the agreed contribution (subject to the fraud exception), and the private company caps a member's exposure at whatever remains unpaid on his shares (often zero, if shares are fully paid-up).

How does registration compare across a partnership firm, an LLP, and a private company - is registration mandatory in each case, and can each entity sue third parties in its own name?

options.A: Registration is mandatory for all three structures - partnership firm, LLP, and private company alike - with no structure permitting voluntary or unregistered operation under any circumstance
options.B: Registration of a partnership firm is VOLUNTARY (an unregistered firm can still exist, though with litigation disabilities), and only a REGISTERED partnership firm can sue third parties; registration of an LLP is MANDATORY (an LLP is created by the legal process of registration under the LLP Act, 2008, and is a body corporate from registration), and an LLP can sue and be sued in its own name; registration of a private company is likewise MANDATORY under the Companies Act, 2013, and a company can sue and be sued in its own name
options.C: Registration is voluntary for all three structures, including the LLP and the private company, since only partnership firms are subject to any registration requirement under Indian law
options.D: An unregistered partnership firm can sue third parties in its own name on exactly the same footing as a registered firm, an LLP, or a private company, since registration status is irrelevant to litigation capacity

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Registration of a partnership firm is VOLUNTARY (an unregistered firm can still exist, though with litigation disabilities), and only a REGISTERED partnership firm can sue third parties; registration of an LLP is MANDATORY (an LLP is created by the legal process of registration under the LLP Act, 2008, and is a body corporate from registration), and an LLP can sue and be sued in its own name; registration of a private company is likewise MANDATORY under the Companies Act, 2013, and a company can sue and be sued in its own name

The registration comparison highlights a partnership firm's distinctive voluntariness - Aditi, Bilal, and Chetan could technically operate an unregistered partnership firm (albeit with the well-known litigation handicap of being unable to sue third parties), whereas both the LLP and private company routes require mandatory registration as a precondition to the entity's very existence as a body corporate, with full suing/being-sued capacity flowing automatically from that registration.

What are the minimum and maximum numbers of partners/members applicable to an LLP and to a private company, respectively, that Aditi, Bilal, and Chetan should consider?

options.B: An LLP has a maximum cap of 50 partners (mirroring the erstwhile private company member limit), while a private company has no maximum limit on its number of members at all
options.C: An LLP requires a minimum of 2 partners, with NO statutory maximum limit on the number of partners; a private company requires a minimum of 2 members, with a MAXIMUM of 200 members under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: An LLP requires a minimum of 7 partners (mirroring the public company minimum), while a private company requires a minimum of only 1 member under all circumstances

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) An LLP requires a minimum of 2 partners, with NO statutory maximum limit on the number of partners; a private company requires a minimum of 2 members, with a MAXIMUM of 200 members under the Companies Act, 2013

This is a meaningful practical consideration for a growing consultancy - the LLP route imposes only a 2-partner floor with no ceiling at all on growth in partner numbers, whereas the private company route, while also starting at a 2-member floor, caps out at 200 members, a distinction the three friends should factor in in light of any future plans to bring in additional co-owners.
